Let us imagine that, at birth, we are given a choice. A major life decision. You can choose to be guaranteed to be involved in a reasonably happy arranged relationship/marriage with a significant other. It will be guaranteed that this person will allow you reasonable happiness (however you define that), but it will not be passionate true love. Or you can choose to roll the dice, and gamble on whether or not you will find your soul mate and experience passionate, true love. Would you roll the dice for true love?

Once you make the decision, it is final. The arrangement will provide you with a reasonable amount of happiness. For the sake of argument, let us say that by gambling, you are literally rolling a pair of dice. You have a one-out-of-twelve (approx. 8.4%) chance of being united with your soul mate, a person that will allow you to experience indescribable true love.

Is it better to take the guarantee? Is life worth living without experiencing the truest of true love? Is it better to play it safe and settle, or gamble for something more? Is there such a thing as soul males and true love in the first place? Would you be gambling on something that is impossible with a "loaded die?"

I am definitely in the camp for arranged marriage. What can I say? I like to play it safe, and I personally would not view an arranged marriage that brings me happiness as "settling" (though I know some people would). I also don't believe in soul mates (though I know people do). I don't want to roll the dice on this one. Give me the consolation prize.
Q: Would you roll the dice for true love?

I do not understand the question. To restate, I do not understand the difference between reasonable happiness and 'soul mate.' Maybe it was because I was raised in a household with unhappy parents, but reasonably happy sounds pretty damn good to me. Life takes work, relationships take work. I would hate to be with someone where I never felt I had to be a better man, and I would hate to be in a relationship where I always thought he was the perfect man. Personal progress takes time and effort, so I guess I would take the guarantee.

Think of it this way: to be in a reasonably happy relationship would mean that you are with someone, and sometimes you might have disagreements about things, but for the most part, this person is someone who you are happy to have as a significant other. But to have a soul mate would mean you could be on Cloud 9 all of the time. You would be star-crossed lovers like Romeo and Juliet. Meant to be. To paraphrase a quote from Jerry Maguire, they "complete you."

That sounds terrible. I would hate to be with someone where I am on Cloud 9 all of the time. The thing that creates beauty is not the perfections, but the mild imperfections. I would still not role the dice. I would roll the dice if the opposite was true.

I think maybe you should consider it from the perspective of: your soul mate wouldn't be perfect, but would be perfect for you.

"Cloud 9" is a very subjective term, and means different things to different people, and I suppose what I was driving at was that, this "soul mate" would be someone that would bring you the most ideal life experience, whatever that may be, instead of just a "hey, it's not so bad, I can live with this" experience.

You can only judge when you are happy if you have unhappiness to compare it to. I would go for a 'normal' relationship, warts and all

On the other hand, if I agree to Happy Marriage, I may be pretty happy overall, but constantly bothered by whether I missed out. I could get over it, but I'd always have a subtle nagging there.

If the dice assure me that it's possible to have this insanely amazing true love experience, and that it will last until one of us dies, you know, hopefully not until many years have passed, that's enough for me. I like to think of these things with a cost-benefit analysis.

How often will you use the computer? - Probably the same whether you get an i5 or i7.

How long will you use it for? - The i7 could potentially add some time of use before the next upgrade. So instead of upgrading in 3 years, maybe its 4 or 5? So $100 savings / 3 years = $33 per year saved. Or if you buy the i7 keep it for 5 years, $100 / 5 = $20 per year spent.

Will you get more joy out of having it? That's up to you.

I would spend the $100 myself, but I'm a power-user.

It depends, what you are using your computer for. If this is primarily gaming then the hyper-threading of an i7 will be of little use to you. Unless you stream as a career and do heavy video editing, I don't think an i7 is necessary. Hyper-threading will have a benefit to video editing, but streaming is more reliant on your GPU for transcoding and your internet connection for latency.
